questions.q: Why is a single DELETE statement against tens of millions of qualifying rows a genuine production risk, per this lesson?
options: It runs as one long transaction, holding locks and log space for the entire duration, and if killed partway through, the entire operation rolls back, undoing all the work
DELETE statements are limited to 1,000 rows per execution and will silently fail on larger tables
SQL Server automatically converts large DELETEs into a TRUNCATE, losing the WHERE clause filter
It is not actually a risk; a single DELETE is always the most efficient approach regardless of row count
questions.explain: One giant transaction holds locks and accumulates log records for the whole operation, and a rollback undoes everything already deleted.

questions.q: What is the TOP (n) loop pattern used for?
options: Breaking a large DELETE or UPDATE into many small, bounded transactions that each commit before the next batch runs, repeating until no rows remain
Selecting only the first n rows of a table for reporting purposes
Forcing a query to use a specific execution plan
Automatically rebuilding indexes after a large data load
questions.explain: The loop repeatedly deletes (or updates) a bounded chunk, commits it as its own small transaction, and checks whether any rows remain.

questions.q: In the TOP (n) loop pattern, what is @@ROWCOUNT used for?
options: Capturing how many rows the last DELETE/UPDATE TOP (n) affected, so the loop knows when zero rows remain and can stop
Setting the batch size dynamically based on server memory
Counting how many times the loop has executed
Locking the exact number of rows specified before the batch begins
questions.explain: @@ROWCOUNT reports the number of rows affected by the last statement; when it reaches zero, the loop has nothing left to process and exits.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what actually changes when a large delete is batched instead of run as one statement?
options: Locks are held briefly per batch instead of for the whole operation, and the transaction log only has to hold one batch's worth of records at a time instead of accumulating for the entire job
The total number of rows deleted is reduced
The WHERE clause filter no longer needs to be specified
SQL Server automatically parallelizes each batch across all available cores
questions.explain: Batching bounds both lock duration and per-transaction log footprint to one batch at a time, rather than the whole multi-million-row operation.

questions.q: How should you choose a batch size for a TOP (n) loop, per this lesson?
options: Pick a starting size, measure its actual effect on blocking and log growth, then adjust — the same measure/identify/change/verify loop from Lesson 1, not a number copied from elsewhere
Always use the largest batch size the server's memory allows
Always use a batch size of exactly 1 row for maximum safety
Batch size never matters; any value produces identical performance
questions.explain: There's no universally correct batch size — it depends on the table, indexing, and concurrent load, so it has to be measured and adjusted rather than assumed.
